The protesters, operating under the March and March movement, confronted Nigerian residents in Sunnyside, a Pretoria suburb with a sizeable Nigerian population, during a demonstration on Wednesday against the presence of foreign nationals in the country.
Leading the protest, the movement’s leader, Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma, demanded an explanation from Nigerians over how the neighbourhood acquired the nickname, insisting that no one had given them permission to identify parts of South Africa with Nigeria.
“I am being told here that we’ve entered Sunnyside, the home of Nigerians. I am inviting Nigerians to come out, let’s talk to each other. We want to know who gave you this place and called it Nigeria. Who gave you permission to call this place Lagos or whatever you call it?” she asked.
Her remarks came as demonstrators intensified their campaign against Nigerian nationals, accusing them of involvement in drug trafficking and contributing to social problems in South African communities.
Ngobese-Zuma described the presence of migrants in the country as “not sustainable and not feasible”, alleging that they were putting additional pressure on public resources and worsening the frustrations of South African citizens.
The movement said it would present its grievances to the Department of Home Affairs, demanding tougher immigration controls, restrictions on refugee admissions and the accelerated deportation of undocumented foreign nationals.
The group’s legal representative, Xolani Zuma, also called for an outright ban on Nigerians entering South Africa, accusing them of selling drugs to South Africans.
“The state must ban Nigerians from South Africa. They must ban Nigerians until they stop selling drugs to our people. The rest of Africa, we are fine, but we do not want Nigerians in South Africa anymore. That is what we are saying,” he declared.
The demonstrators further urged the South African government to withdraw from the 1951 United Nations Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees, arguing that the country’s obligations under the international agreement were no longer sustainable.
The latest demonstration comes amid renewed tensions between Nigeria and South Africa over recurring xenophobic hostility, the safety of Nigerian nationals and disagreements surrounding diplomatic relations between both countries.
Last week, Nigeria’s High Commissioner to South Africa, Femi Fani-Kayode, was involved in a diplomatic disagreement with the South African Presidency following the exclusion of his prepared speech during the presentation of his credentials.
Fani-Kayode described the omission as disrespectful to Nigeria but subsequently announced that the disagreement had been resolved following the intervention of South African President Cyril Ramaphosa and an invitation from the country’s Department of International Relations and Cooperation.
The Nigerian envoy also disclosed that he had begun addressing concerns affecting Nigerians living in South Africa since assuming office.
He described those responsible for xenophobic attacks as a tiny minority who should not be allowed to define the character of South Africa, maintaining that the majority of the country’s citizens were decent and accommodating.
Fani-Kayode expressed confidence that Nigeria and South Africa could overcome their differences without severing their longstanding diplomatic relations.
However, he warned that patience was running thin within Nigeria’s corridors of power over repeated attacks on its citizens, insisting that the country would not abandon its nationals to xenophobic violence.
